newsitem.title: UK: BA to suffer as travelers switch airlines.
newsitem.headline: BA to suffer as travelers switch airlines.

text.p: British Airways Plc, hit by a 72-hour strike by its cabin crews, could face long-term damage as passengers switch to rival companies, industry analysts said Wednesday.

Other operators on British Airways routes said they increased seat capacity and added flights to accommodate passengers grounded by the first day of the strike. But the Association of Independent Tour Operators said there was virtually no availability on alternative flights on the worst-affected routes.
"There is a lot of juggling going on, and it is chaotic," an AITO spokeswoman said.
BA said it cancelled 135 flights from its main hub at London's Heathrow airport on Wednesday, 69 percent of the total scheduled.

The airline said the strike was unlawful and threatened to take legal action unless the union involved accepted the terms of its pay offer, aimed at cutting costs by 42 million pounds ($70.9 million). It set a Wednesday afternoon deadline.

An airline official said discrepancies in a strike ballot of British Airlines' Stewards and Stewardesses Association members had rendered the strike illegal. He said that if the union did not halt the strike, BA would be entitled to seek compensation for the losses it incurred.
Some analysts believe British Airways lost around 25 million pounds ($42 million) in bookings before the 72-hour strike started.

Some estimates put the cost to the airline of lost sales, refunding tickets, switching passengers to other airlines and paying temporary staff at up to 20 million pounds ($33 million) for every day the strike continues.
Last year even the threat of a pilots strike cost BA 15 million pounds ($25 million), without a flight being cancelled.

"It's incredibly difficult to put a financial estimate on it but with a three-day strike ... we could be talking several times that 15 million, even if it is only the three-day strike and doesn't go on next week," said Chris Avery, airlines analyst at Parisbas bank.

Rival airlines,including the non-union British Midland, Virgin Atlantic, Air UK and Deutsche Lufthansa AG, reported strong rises in bookings as passengers sought to avoid the uncertainty of booking on BA.

British Midland said it put larger aircraft on some routes and had seen bookings rise on routes such as London to Edinburgh and Belfast, where it competes directly with BA. Air UK said it added flights from London to Edinburgh, Glasgow and Amsterdam.
German flag carrier Lufthansa said Tuesday it would add capacity and flights between London and major German cities, and Virgin Atlantic said all its seats were sold up to Sunday.

Virgin said it was adding two flights between London and New York on Friday evening to cope with demand. It also reported a "large increase" in bookings for its UK train service, Virgin Rail, which serves Glasgow and Manchester.
AITO said the dispute was "hammering" independent holiday operators.
"There will be people having problems with their holidays, and our tour operators are working hard at finding alternative routings," a spokeswoman said.
But the biggest threat to BA could be the loss of premium-paying business travelers, who may prove hard to lure back once they have switched to rivals.

"This is a very competitive industry where there are plenty of alternatives," said Paribas's Avery. "Having been disrupted once in a pretty significant way by a strike at British Airways you are going to find people drift off to other carriers (and) quite like the service, and then BA's got a hell of a job to get them back."
